paragraphs: AdaBelief addresses a familiar tension in neural network training: adaptive optimizers often learn quickly, while momentum-based stochastic gradient descent can generalize better. Some settings, including generative adversarial networks, also place a premium on training stability. The paper proposes an optimizer intended to combine these strengths by changing how it decides whether to trust a gradient.

Its reference point is an exponential moving average of recent gradients, interpreted as a prediction of the next gradient. When the observed gradient differs substantially from that prediction, AdaBelief reduces the step size. When observation and prediction agree, it permits a larger step. The central idea is that agreement with recent behavior provides a useful signal for choosing the size of an update.

The reported experiments show fast convergence and high accuracy on image classification and language modeling. On ImageNet, accuracy is comparable to SGD. In a Cifar10 GAN experiment, AdaBelief also provides stable training and better generated samples than a well-tuned Adam optimizer. These findings support the proposed combination of speed, generalization, and stability in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-adabelief-optimizer-adaptin.tldr: AdaBelief adjusts update sizes according to how closely observed gradients match their predictions, with reported benefits for convergence, accuracy, and stability.

paragraphs: Learning a dynamic model from observations involves predicting how a system changes over successive steps. For estimation and control, the behavior of those predictions over time matters alongside their agreement with data. This paper develops neural network dynamic models whose construction includes a provable stability guarantee, focusing on discrete-time systems that may contain randomness.

The key component is a Lyapunov neural network embedded within the dynamic model. A Lyapunov function provides a way to establish stability through a mathematical criterion. By incorporating that criterion into the model, the method makes stability part of the learned system's structure. The paper presents two ways to do this: one uses convexity of the Lyapunov function, while the other imposes stability through an implicit output layer.

Both approaches are applied to deterministic and stochastic settings, and numerical examples demonstrate their utility. The contribution is a way to combine flexible neural models with stability requirements during learning. This addresses the challenge of maintaining a guarantee when both discrete time and stochastic behavior complicate the dynamics.
neurips-2020-almost-surely-stable-deep-d.tldr: The paper embeds learned Lyapunov functions into neural dynamic models to guarantee stability in deterministic and stochastic settings.

paragraphs: Language generation trained by maximum likelihood can suffer from a mismatch between training and generation, and from treating a single reference text as the only correct answer. Adversarial training could help address these issues, but discrete text makes it difficult to apply. Earlier reinforcement learning approaches to language GANs had underperformed maximum likelihood training.

This paper focuses on exploration: how the generator samples text while learning. The authors show that a popular sampling method produces unstable training. Their alternative, ColdGANs, keeps sampled outputs closer to the mode of the generator's distribution, meaning the region it currently considers most likely. This more cautious sampling produces smoother learning dynamics and makes exploration a central design choice.

Experiments cover unconditional text generation, question generation, and abstractive summarization. The authors report favorable comparisons with maximum likelihood and improvements over the state of the art on the evaluated tasks. They describe the favorable language-GAN comparison as a first to their knowledge. The findings connect the choice of sampling strategy to whether adversarial language training works effectively.
neurips-2020-coldgans-taming-language-ga.tldr: ColdGANs stabilizes adversarial text generation through cautious sampling, improving results on three evaluated language tasks.

paragraphs: Larger neural networks often perform better, and Neural Tangent Kernel theory connects some of that improvement to an optimization landscape that is easier to navigate. This paper investigates another way to increase model capacity: aggregate several independent networks with identical architectures and train their combination as one model. The authors call this construction a collegial ensemble.

As the number of component models becomes large, the ensemble's optimization dynamics simplify and resemble those of wide networks, while scaling more favorably. The paper uses theoretical corrections that account for finite network width to search efficiently over practical ensemble architectures. Depending on the constraints, the search can aim to reduce capacity or improve trainability.

The resulting ensembles can be implemented using group convolutions and block diagonal layers. The framework also analytically recovers optimal group convolution modules that had previously required expensive grid searches, without training a model during that derivation. This connects an analysis of learning dynamics to concrete architecture choices, making theory useful for designing the structure before training begins.
neurips-2020-collegial-ensembles-52730a3.tldr: Collegial ensembles combine identical network architectures into one trainable model and use optimization theory to guide efficient architecture design.

paragraphs: A recommendation platform connects people who consume content with people who produce it. Choosing relevant items for consumers is only one part of understanding the resulting system: providers also make strategic choices about what to create. This paper studies those content creation dynamics through game theory, motivated by the broader problem of serving all participants in a recommendation ecosystem.

Within a previously proposed stylized model, the authors prove that the dynamics always reach a pure Nash equilibrium. At such an equilibrium, no provider can benefit by changing its own strategy alone. However, the path to that outcome can take exponentially long. The result therefore separates eventual stability from the practical speed at which decentralized behavior reaches it.

The paper also develops an efficient algorithm for computing a pure Nash equilibrium through a combinatorial optimization problem. This supplies a computational route to an equilibrium even when the modeled dynamics converge slowly. The guarantee concerns equilibrium in the stated model; convergence itself does not establish that every stakeholder receives high social welfare.
neurips-2020-content-provider-dynamics-a.tldr: In a stylized recommendation ecosystem, provider dynamics always reach equilibrium but may do so slowly, while an efficient algorithm can compute an equilibrium.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning trains a neural network to represent samples as vectors whose relationships express similarity. Angular losses compare vector directions, separating direction from magnitude and aligning the measures used during training and testing. Yet these losses do not necessarily keep all training vectors at the same distance from the origin.

The paper investigates why those varying lengths matter even when similarity is defined through angles. Unequal embedding norms can lead to unstable gradients within a batch and may slow convergence. The proposed spherical embedding constraint regulates the distribution of vector lengths, adaptively bringing embeddings onto a shared hypersphere. This produces more balanced updates to their directions, which are the quantities used by angular comparison.

Experiments evaluate the approach in deep metric learning, face recognition, and contrastive self-supervised learning. The authors report significant performance improvements over the state of the art in these evaluations. The contribution identifies vector length as an important part of optimizing directional representations and provides a constraint designed to address its effect on learning.
neurips-2020-deep-metric-learning-with-s.tldr: A spherical embedding constraint regulates vector lengths to balance angular learning updates and improve performance across three evaluated learning settings.

paragraphs: Accelerated MRI collects only part of the measurements available in the Fourier domain. Deciding which measurements to acquire is an experimental design problem, and existing strategies rely mainly on heuristics. This paper instead learns acquisition strategies using policy gradient methods, treating the measurement design as a policy that can be improved through training.

The experiments compare a general non-greedy approach with a simpler greedy approximation of its objective. Unexpectedly, the greedy version produces solutions nearly as good as those of the more general approach. The authors offer a partial explanation: gradient estimates for the non-greedy objective have greater variance, making the training signal less consistent.

Further experiments show that this variance interferes with the non-greedy models' ability to adapt their policies to individual MR images. Such adaptation is empirically important for improving measurement designs. The result highlights a tension between a more general objective and how effectively that objective can be learned. In these experiments, a simpler approximation retains much of the performance while supporting useful image-specific adaptation.
neurips-2020-experimental-design-for-mri.tldr: Learned greedy MRI sampling performs nearly as well as a more general approach, partly because noisier gradients hinder the latter's adaptation to individual images.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses existing experience to learn policies when direct exploration is costly or infeasible. Practical adoption can be difficult when the resulting decisions are hard to interpret and the method does not express uncertainty about their value. Expert-Supervised Reinforcement Learning addresses these issues by making uncertainty quantification part of offline policy learning.

The framework uses hypothesis testing to learn safe and optimal policies and supports different degrees of risk aversion for different applications. It also represents uncertainty through posterior distributions, providing a way to interpret the policy at each state. The same framework computes posterior distributions over off-policy value functions, so evaluation includes uncertainty about the value of a policy.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for its estimators and regret bounds consistent with Posterior Sampling for Reinforcement Learning. It further states that sample efficiency is independent of the chosen risk aversion threshold and the quality of the behavior policy that generated the data. Together, these contributions connect policy learning, uncertainty-aware evaluation, and adjustable risk preferences within one framework.
neurips-2020-expert-supervised-reinforce.tldr: ESRL uses uncertainty estimates and hypothesis testing to support interpretable offline policy learning with adjustable risk aversion and theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: The Langevin algorithm is a method for sampling from a distribution described through a function f, with probability density proportional to exp(-f). Understanding how quickly it approaches that target distribution is important in high-dimensional sampling. This paper studies the case where the function is defined on a manifold, a space whose geometry need not be ordinary Euclidean geometry.

The work extends an earlier convergence analysis from Euclidean space to this manifold setting. Its central result concerns Kullback–Leibler divergence, a measure of discrepancy between the sampling distribution and the target. The authors show that this discrepancy decreases at a geometric rate whenever the target distribution satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality on the manifold.

The log-Sobolev condition is central to the stated guarantee: the result does not assert fast convergence for every manifold distribution. Its significance is that convergence can be analyzed using a property of the distribution together with the geometry of its domain. This broadens the theoretical setting for fast Langevin sampling beyond functions defined on ordinary vector spaces.
neurips-2020-fast-convergence-of-langevi.tldr: Langevin sampling on a manifold achieves geometric decay in KL divergence when the target distribution satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated games in which players choose among n actions for T rounds using Hedge or its optimistic variant. Regret measures the advantage of alternative choices in hindsight. External regret compares against a fixed action, while swap regret considers replacing each chosen action according to a consistent mapping. Lower regret also connects learning behavior to game-theoretic equilibrium.

For two-player games, the authors improve the optimistic Hedge regret decay bound to roughly T^(-5/6), suppressing logarithmic factors, from the previous T^(-3/4) bound. They also show that ordinary Hedge cannot generally improve beyond a roughly T^(-1/2) rate. This establishes a theoretical separation between the two methods in this setting.

For m-player games, combining optimistic Hedge with a standard regret reduction yields swap regret decay of roughly m^(1/2)(n/T)^(3/4). A modification retains that rate in self-play and achieves roughly sqrt(n/T) against adversaries. Through standard connections between regret and equilibrium, the upper bounds imply faster convergence to coarse correlated equilibria for two players and correlated equilibria for multiple players.
neurips-2020-hedging-in-games-faster-con.tldr: The paper proves faster regret decay for optimistic Hedge in repeated games and establishes a slower worst-case rate for ordinary Hedge.

paragraphs: Co-saliency detection identifies visually important content shared across images. It relies on evidence about what stands out within each image and what corresponds across the collection. The paper argues that existing learned methods emphasize relationships between images while making insufficient use of saliency information already available within individual images.

ICNet starts from single-image saliency maps produced by an off-the-shelf detector. A normalized masked average pooling operation combines these maps with semantic features to extract latent saliency categories. A correlation fusion module then compares these internal cues with single-image features to obtain information about shared content. This makes within-image saliency an explicit input to reasoning about relationships across images.

The method also introduces a category-independent rearranged self-correlation feature strategy to improve detection. Experiments on three benchmarks show better co-saliency performance than previous state-of-the-art methods, and ablation studies support the effectiveness of the proposed components. The findings indicate that explicitly organizing and correlating single-image saliency cues can strengthen the detection of common salient content.
neurips-2020-icnet-intra-saliency-correl.tldr: ICNet uses saliency within individual images to build stronger cross-image cues, outperforming previous co-saliency methods on three benchmarks.

paragraphs: Bayesian phylogenetic inference estimates uncertainty about evolutionary trees, including their branching structure and branch lengths. Variational Bayesian phylogenetic inference approximates these posterior distributions efficiently. The paper identifies a restriction in the existing approach: its diagonal Lognormal approximation for branch lengths limits how richly it can represent the posterior.

The proposed VBPI-NF method replaces that restrictive family with more flexible distributions built using normalizing flows. These transformations must accommodate branch length spaces associated with different tree structures. Carefully designed permutation equivariant transformations handle this geometry while allowing the learned distribution family to generalize across tree topologies. Their structure makes the method compatible with changes in the organization of the tree.

On a benchmark of challenging Bayesian phylogenetic problems using real data, VBPI-NF significantly improves on the original VBPI method. Further analysis finds that the structured transformations can provide additional amortization benefits, allowing learning to be shared across inference cases. The contribution therefore combines a more expressive approximation with a design that respects the structure of the phylogenetic problem.
neurips-2020-improved-variational-bayesi.tldr: VBPI-NF uses structure-aware normalizing flows to improve branch length posterior approximations across evolutionary tree topologies.

paragraphs: This paper combines machine learning with compartmental disease modeling to forecast the progression of COVID-19. Compartmental models, such as SEIR, describe disease dynamics through changes among population groups. The proposed approach retains that explicit structure while using machine learning to incorporate covariates and improve forecasting performance.

Interpretability is built into two parts of the model. Its outputs show how the compartments evolve, and interpretable encoders provide a way to incorporate additional variables. This design gives users access to an account of the predicted progression alongside the forecast itself. The authors emphasize the value of such explanations for epidemiologists evaluating credibility and for policymakers and healthcare institutions using the forecasts.

The model supports different geographic resolutions, with demonstrations for United States states and counties. The authors report more accurate forecasts than the alternatives they evaluate and explanatory insights that are qualitatively meaningful. The stated contribution is therefore a combination of predictive performance and interpretable disease dynamics, with evidence that this combination works at both of the demonstrated geographic scales.
neurips-2020-interpretable-sequence-lear.tldr: The paper combines compartmental disease models with interpretable machine learning to improve COVID-19 forecasts and explain their predicted dynamics.

paragraphs: Immune repertoire classification predicts an individual's immune status from a vast collection of immune receptor sequences. This is a multiple instance learning problem: the prediction belongs to the collection, while useful evidence may appear in only a very small fraction of its members. The paper addresses collections two orders of magnitude larger than previously considered problems.

The authors connect transformer attention to the update rule of modern Hopfield networks, which can store exponentially many patterns. Their DeepRC method incorporates this attention mechanism into a deep learning architecture for massive collections. The connection provides the basis for using high-capacity pattern storage and retrieval in a setting where relevant sequences are rare.

Large-scale experiments include simulated data and real-world virus infection data. DeepRC outperforms the other evaluated methods in predictive performance and can extract sequence motifs associated with a disease class. Those motifs add an interpretable view of the patterns connected to predictions. The paper frames accurate, interpretable repertoire classification as a possible contributor to future vaccines and therapies, rather than demonstrating those downstream outcomes.
neurips-2020-modern-hopfield-networks-an.tldr: DeepRC uses the connection between attention and modern Hopfield networks to classify massive immune repertoires and extract disease-associated sequence motifs.

paragraphs: Tracking a deforming object requires finding how its surface moves between observations. This paper takes two RGB-D frames, which contain color and depth information, and uses a convolutional network to predict dense correspondences between them. The network also assigns confidence values to those matches, allowing the tracker to distinguish more trustworthy constraints from questionable ones.

The correspondences feed into an as-rigid-as-possible optimization problem that estimates the object's non-rigid motion. The key design choice is to make the weighted nonlinear least-squares solver differentiable. Training can then propagate through the optimization, so the predicted matches and confidence values are learned for their usefulness to the final tracking task. Confidence learning can use self-supervision, automatically reducing the influence of outliers and incorrect matches.

The authors report improved reconstruction performance compared with state-of-the-art approaches. They also report correspondence prediction that is 85 times faster than comparable deep learning methods. That speed claim concerns correspondence prediction specifically. Together, the results support integrating learned matching and robust optimization into a single trainable tracking system.
neurips-2020-neural-non-rigid-tracking-f.tldr: A differentiable tracker jointly learns surface matches and their confidence, improving non-rigid reconstruction while greatly accelerating correspondence prediction.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using data collected under another policy. Such estimates can become biased when unrecorded variables influence both past decisions and their outcomes. This paper develops worst-case performance bounds to assess how robust policy evaluations remain under this hidden confounding.

The authors show that even small amounts of confounding at every decision can produce substantial bias over an episode. They then study a narrower model: hidden confounders directly affect only one decision, with later effects passing through that decision. Under this assumption, they develop an efficient procedure based on loss minimization to compute worst-case bounds and prove its statistical consistency.

Simulated healthcare examples involve sepsis management and interventions for autistic children, where the authors consider the one-decision model reasonable. The method both rejects conclusions from non-robust evaluations and provides meaningful robustness certificates. These results show how the bounds can support policy selection while making the assumed structure of hidden confounding central to the evaluation.
neurips-2020-off-policy-policy-evaluatio.tldr: The paper bounds policy performance under hidden confounding, with an efficient consistent method when confounding directly affects only one decision.

paragraphs: Geometric perception often has to estimate shapes, poses, or alignments from measurements containing many outliers. Truncated least squares limits the influence of those outliers, but its objective is difficult to optimize because it is nonconvex and nonsmooth. This paper develops a general framework for solving such problems and certifying the quality of candidate solutions.

For a broad class of perception problems, the authors reformulate the objective using polynomials and apply convex moment relaxations. At the minimum relaxation order, these are empirically tight, yielding certified global minima in the reported cases. Exploiting polynomial sparsity and reducing the basis makes the resulting semidefinite programs substantially smaller without sacrificing tightness.

A complementary approach checks solutions produced by other methods, including fast heuristics. These dual certifiers compute a suboptimality gap and may establish global optimality; certification is not promised for every candidate. Experiments across rotation estimation, alignment, registration, and satellite pose estimation demonstrate tight relaxations and correct certification. The proposed certifiers also scale to problems beyond the reach of current semidefinite programming solvers.
neurips-2020-one-ring-to-rule-them-all-c.tldr: Polynomial relaxations and scalable certifiers enable robust geometric estimation with measurable solution quality and, in demonstrated cases, certified global optimality.

paragraphs: Repeatedly aggregating information across a graph can make node representations overly similar, a problem called over-smoothing. Multi-scale graph neural networks are a promising response, but their empirical success has lacked a clear learning-theoretic explanation. This paper analyzes optimization and generalization for transductive learning algorithms that include these networks.

The authors use boosting theory to establish convergence of training error under weak learning-type conditions. They combine this analysis with generalization gap bounds expressed through transductive Rademacher complexity. For a particular type of multi-scale graph network, the resulting test error bound decreases as the number of node aggregations increases, provided certain conditions hold. The conclusion therefore concerns a specified architecture and conditional bound.

This gives a theoretical account of how multi-scale structure can help counter over-smoothing while benefiting from further aggregation. The authors also train multi-scale networks using boosting algorithms on real-world node prediction tasks. Performance is comparable to existing graph neural networks, and the observed practical behavior agrees with their theoretical analysis. The empirical finding supports the explanation without claiming universal superiority.
neurips-2020-optimization-and-generaliza.tldr: Boosting-based analysis gives conditional optimization and generalization guarantees explaining why multi-scale graph networks can resist over-smoothing.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning replaces numerical rewards with judgments about which outcomes or trajectories are preferable. This can help express an objective when assigning reward numbers is difficult. The paper develops a finite-time theoretical analysis, addressing how such feedback can support the identification of a good decision policy.

The authors first show that deterministic preferences over trajectories may fail to produce a unique optimal policy. Their positive guarantees use stochastic preferences whose probabilities are related to hidden reward values. Under that relationship, they provide algorithms both with and without a simulator that identify a policy within a specified accuracy of the best one with high probability.

The method deliberately navigates toward under-explored states and combines policy search with dueling bandits, which learn from comparisons. This connects the need to gather informative experience with the need to decide which behavior is preferable. Experiments on real-world problems demonstrate the method's efficacy. The theoretical contribution is conditional on the stated preference model, clarifying when comparison feedback supports reliable policy learning.
neurips-2020-preference-based-reinforcem.tldr: Under a stochastic preference model linked to hidden rewards, the paper gives finite-time guarantees for learning an approximately optimal policy.

paragraphs: Foraging involves repeatedly deciding whether to remain with a diminishing resource or leave for another opportunity. The marginal value theorem describes average stay-or-leave behavior well, but leaves questions about how individual choices are learned. This paper uses interpretable deep actor-critic models to investigate R-learning as a possible learning mechanism for those decisions.

The models predict choice patterns consistent with mice performing foraging tasks. Their temporal-difference error, the signal used to train the model, correlates with dopamine activity in ventral tegmental area neurons. Theoretical and experimental results show that the learned agents leave when the current reward intake rate falls below an exponential average of rates from past trials.

That rule describes individual decisions while matching the marginal value theorem on average, connecting reinforcement learning with behavioral ecology. The authors further argue that the rule is Bayes optimal in dynamic real-world environments. The biological evidence establishes consistency and correlation, supporting a proposed mechanism rather than proving that animals implement the model. The contribution links learning, observed behavior, and established decision theories.
neurips-2020-r-learning-in-actor-critic-.tldr: Deep R-learning produces a stay-or-leave rule consistent with mouse foraging behavior and connects individual choices to average-case foraging theory.

paragraphs: Variants of Frank-Wolfe can converge at a linear rate when minimizing smooth convex functions over polytopes under a quadratic growth assumption. However, established rates explicitly depend on the dimension of the entire problem. This paper asks whether a solution lying on a much smaller face of the feasible polytope can justify a better guarantee.

The authors first show that a low-dimensional optimal face alone is insufficient: even simple problems can require dependence on the full dimension in the worst case. They then add a strict complementarity assumption. Under this condition, Frank-Wolfe with away-steps and line search converges linearly at a rate whose explicit dimensional dependence involves only the optimal face.

This can substantially improve the bound when the solution is sparse, because its relevant face may be much smaller than the full problem. The paper also shows that strict complementarity implies robustness of solution sparsity to noise. That result motivates the extra assumption and explains why sparse structure can support faster guarantees when it is accompanied by the required stability property.
neurips-2020-revisiting-frank-wolfe-for-.tldr: With strict complementarity, away-step Frank-Wolfe has a linear convergence rate whose explicit dimensional dependence is on the optimal face.

paragraphs: Meta-learning trains models to adapt quickly to new tasks, usually by optimizing average performance over a task distribution. This can give insufficient attention to rare or difficult tasks. The paper reformulates Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning to minimize the largest loss among the observed training tasks, making worst-case task performance the objective.

Controlling that maximum protects performance across different distributions over the observed tasks. This provides robustness when their relative frequencies change between training and testing. The scope matters: the distributional protection is over the observed tasks. The paper separately supplies an upper bound on generalization error for new tasks that captures an advantage of minimizing the worst-case loss.

The authors give an algorithm for the resulting min-max problem. In convex settings, it reaches an epsilon-accurate point at the optimal rate O(1/epsilon²). In nonconvex settings, it reaches an (epsilon, delta)-stationary point at rate O(max{1/epsilon⁵, 1/delta⁵}), a different type of guarantee. Sinusoid regression and image classification experiments demonstrate the advantage of the proposed objective.
neurips-2020-task-robust-model-agnostic-.tldr: Task-robust MAML minimizes the worst observed task loss to protect against shifts in task frequencies, with theoretical and experimental support.

paragraphs: Tensor completion reconstructs a low-rank multidimensional array from a sparse subset of its entries. Existing approaches face a difficult tradeoff: some are practical but heuristic, others require large semidefinite programs, and some depend on strong assumptions such as nearly orthogonal factors. This paper proposes a variant of alternating minimization that combines practical computation with theoretical guarantees.

The method comes from examining how measures of progress used in matrix completion must change for tensors. That analysis leads to a modification of the standard alternating procedure. The authors prove linear convergence to the true tensor even when its factors are highly correlated, and show that the method can be implemented in nearly linear time.

The practical evaluation demonstrates completion of third-order tensors with a thousand dimensions while observing only a tiny fraction of their entries. The authors also find that ordinary alternating minimization can converge drastically more slowly in practice. The findings make the modification consequential both for the convergence theory and for the efficiency of actual tensor recovery.
neurips-2020-tensor-completion-made-prac.tldr: A modified alternating minimization method offers provable, practical tensor completion even with highly correlated factors.

paragraphs: ImageNet-trained convolutional networks often classify ambiguous images using texture rather than shape. This paper investigates whether that tendency reflects an inherent difficulty learning shape. When trained on images whose shape and texture conflict, the networks learn shape-based classification at least as easily as texture-based classification, showing that they can readily use shape in that setting.

The authors then vary architectures, unsupervised objectives, and data augmentation. Architecture and objective changes have small but significant, largely independent effects, yet the tested models still mostly choose texture. Shape can remain decodable from their internal representations even when it does not drive the final classification, separating the presence of information from its use.

Changing augmentation has a much larger effect. Less aggressive random cropping, together with color distortion, noise, and blur, produces models that favor shape on most ambiguous images and outperform baselines on out-of-distribution tests. The findings suggest that apparent differences between human and network image processing may arise primarily from differences in experienced data, rather than internal mechanisms.
neurips-2020-the-origins-and-prevalence-.tldr: The experiments suggest that training data augmentation strongly shapes CNN texture bias and can shift decisions toward shape while improving out-of-distribution performance.

paragraphs: Time-reversal symmetry is a property of many physical systems: their dynamics follow the same governing behavior when the time axis is reversed appropriately. This paper uses that property to guide ordinary differential equation networks that learn physical dynamics from observed trajectories. The aim is to make learning more sample-efficient by incorporating a relevant physical structure.

The authors introduce a loss that measures disagreement between the network's forward and backward time evolutions. Training with this loss encourages consistency with time-reversal symmetry. Their resulting framework, Time-Reversal Symmetric ODE Networks, therefore uses the relationship between two directions of evolution as an additional learning signal.

Evaluations on several classical dynamical systems show that the framework can learn the desired evolution from noisy and complex trajectories. The authors also report better predictions than baselines for tested systems that do not have full time-reversal symmetry. This suggests that the proposed loss can remain useful when the symmetry is incomplete, with that extension supported by the reported experiments rather than a claim about every physical system.
neurips-2020-time-reversal-symmetric-ode.tldr: A loss comparing forward and backward dynamics helps ODE networks learn physical trajectories more sample-efficiently, including in tests with incomplete time-reversal symmetry.
